pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (these coincide with the page numbers printed on the preprint)

entry.evidence: since the description of similar forms in any depositional environment is rare in the literature

steps.action: The authors set the aim: document the collapse structures in periglacial eolian sand and interpret how they formed.
steps.quote: The aim of the present research is to provide a detailed documentation of the structures and interpretation of [...]

steps.action: The authors take from the literature (Decker et al. 2005) the Middle Pleistocene to recent transtensional reactivation of the VBTF and its pull-apart basins.
steps.quote: The VBTF experienced transtensional reactivation in this latter phase

steps.action: Using archival reflection seismics and borehole profiles, the authors show that the study site sits above the negative flower structure of the VBTF in the Zohor-Plavecký Basin.
steps.quote: The basin is situated above a negative flower structure of the Vienna Basin transfer fault, as is evident from the reflection seismics (Fig. 3).

steps.action: The authors cite earlier luminescence ages from the sandpit (40 to 13 ka) and earlier brief reports of soft-sediment deformation there.
steps.quote: Soft-sediment deformation structures were first briefly reported from the Bažantnica sandpit by Fordinál et al. (2012a) and by Kadlec et al. (2015)

steps.action: The authors did the fieldwork in sub-zero December conditions so the frozen sand could be cleaned. They picked a main wall for its abundant deformations and its orientation perpendicular to the fractures, measured all fractures and bedding dips with a compass, and sampled the wall for OSL.
steps.quote: selected on the basis of the abundance of deformation structures and on its orientation perpendicular to the brittle deformations

steps.action: The authors described the primary structures (subhorizontal layers, cross-strata, erosional surfaces, granule layers) and measured bedding dips on the main wall and the other walls.
steps.quote: The dip of the strata attains 10–14° in the lower, and 5–8° in the upper part of the main wall

steps.action: From grain shape and stratification the authors inferred deposition on a periglacial eolian sand sheet with wind ripples, small dunes and deflation lags.
steps.quote: indicates deposition from subcritically climbing wind ripples on a sand sheet

steps.action: The authors checked all other eolian sandpits in the Slovak Vienna Basin, which lie off the VBTF trace, for similar deformations and found none.
steps.quote: All other sandpits in eolian sands of the Slovakian part of the Vienna Basin were checked for the presence of similar deformation structures

steps.action: The authors documented the wedge-shaped structures (21 on the main wall, 17 on other walls): their geometry, fills and associated fractures. Fracture dips and strikes are consistent between the main wall and the other walls, oriented N–S to NE–SW, and the wedges are grouped in horizons truncated by erosional surfaces.
steps.quote: Fractures are systematically oriented N–S and NE–SW (Fig. 8).

steps.action: The authors described the chaotic beds, the folded layers, the two types of erosional surfaces and a complex slide-like deformation, all co-occurring in the wedge horizons.
steps.quote: Beds a few centimeters to 15 cm thick with chaotic structure appear frequently

steps.action: The authors dated seven quartz OSL samples with the SAR protocol: gamma-spectrometry dose rates, water content, mean or median equivalent doses chosen from abanico plots. The ages are in stratigraphic order, and PS1 is a possible outlier.
steps.quote: The OSL ages range between 16.7 ± 0.9 ka and 25.9 ± 1.7 ka (Table 1).

steps.action: Reported in Methods: preheat plateau, thermal transfer and dose recovery tests on each sample, plus an IR purity test on every aliquot. Aliquots failing IR, recycling or error criteria were rejected.
steps.quote: indicated that the SAR protocol correctly measured the given dose

steps.action: Because the OSL errors are large relative to the dated span, the authors built a Bayesian Bacon age-depth model (MCMC, continuous deposition assumed) to date horizons in 1 cm steps.
steps.quote: Hence, the Bayesian age-depth model was considered the most robust approach to the determination of the timing of depositional and deformation events.

steps.action: Reported in Methods: the authors varied the Bacon memory prior parameters over a range and found very low output variability, then kept the defaults.
steps.quote: After testing a range of values with very low variability of the output

steps.action: For the wedge mechanism the authors set the earlier water-escape interpretation against opening of extensional (dilation) cracks with collapse, and against faults reaching the surface.
steps.quote: can be readily explained by the opening of extensional (dilation) cracks

steps.action: The authors excluded water escape (it requires upward transport and saturation, while the wedges show downward transport in the vadose zone) and excluded faulting (most fractures lack displacement).
steps.quote: as a general rule, are indicative of a downward transport of material

steps.action: Against the objection that an overhanging fracture wall in loose sand should collapse, the authors add the auxiliary of cohesion from frozen vadose water, supported by cited rheology experiments and LGM paleoclimate. They extend it to explain the chaotic and folded beds.
steps.quote: The rheology of loose sand can be significantly altered by frozen vadose water

steps.action: The authors interpreted the 85 cm complex deformation as compression at the margin of a slide of partly frozen sand.
steps.quote: The observed deformation probably originated in the marginal part of a slide

steps.action: For the trigger the authors consider slope mass movement, periglacial frost or ice wedging, and seismic shock.
steps.quote: The systematic orientation of fractures (Fig. 8) narrows the possible genetic explanations.

steps.action: The authors excluded slope mass movement (fracture strikes are unrelated to bedding dip across walls) and a frost or ice-wedge origin (the fractures are inclined and uniformly oriented).
steps.quote: the formation of the fractures by slope mass movement can be excluded

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the expectation that seismic dilation cracks form above blind faults, oriented relative to the stress axes, and that liquefaction requires M≥5.5.
steps.quote: These ruptures are usually arranged systematically with respect to the orientation of the seismic wave

steps.action: From the absence of water-escape structures the authors infer that the paleo-earthquake magnitudes were below 5.5.
steps.quote: implying that earthquake magnitudes within the area and time interval under investigation were below 5.5

steps.action: The authors built a tentative process-based model of the seismic hypothesis: a shock disturbs the surface layers, fractures open and form collapse wedges, and these are repeated along reactivated fractures and beveled by erosion.
steps.quote: A process-based model of the origin of the deformations described here is illustrated in Figs. 17 and 18.

steps.action: The authors compared the N–S fracture orientation with the cited VBTF kinematic model (sinistral transtension, W–E extension) and found it consistent.
steps.quote: The dominant N-S orientation of documented fractures (Fig. 8) is consistent with the suggested stress field

steps.action: From the Bacon model the authors derived an accumulation rate of 0.196 cm/yr for the main wall.
steps.quote: The linear Bacon age-depth model yielded an accumulation rate of 0.196 cm/year

steps.action: The authors compared the accumulation rate with published sand-sheet accumulation rates worldwide and found it within range.
steps.quote: Hence, the obtained accumulation rate falls within a reasonable range.

steps.action: The authors keep the seismic-shock origin and treat the wedges in one horizon as one event, giving 21 events on the main wall.
steps.quote: The deformations described herein are considered to have been formed by a seismic shock.

steps.action: The authors assigned Bacon ages to the 21 deformed horizons and computed the intervals between events. They identify a fully exposed quiescence gap and a partly covered gap.
steps.quote: The recurrence period of deformation events is generally between 40 and 190 years, with a mean value of 142.6 ± 114.6 years

steps.action: The authors retain the recurrence estimate as an order of magnitude, noting the bias from age-model uncertainty.
steps.quote: it does nonetheless give an order of magnitude for the recurrence times

tree.answer: Collapse wedges with chaotic and folded beds in Late Pleistocene periglacial eolian sand
Structures observed in outcrop; trigger and timing known only from traces
Document the structures, explain their formation and trigger, and estimate earthquake recurrence
Mechanism: water escape vs dilation collapse vs faulting. Trigger: slope movement vs frost or ice wedge vs seismic shock
Yes: upward vs downward transport; fracture strike relative to bedding; fracture inclination and uniformity
Conditions found in the trace record, not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats: 21 deformed horizons on the main wall plus wedges on the other walls
Partly: consistent orientations on other walls, absence at off-fault sandpits, OSL protocol tests, Bacon parameter test
Seismic trigger kept as best explanation; recurrence of about 143 years with large uncertainty
Not shown: non-peer-reviewed preprint, no review file supplied

end.claim: The collapse wedges, chaotic and folded beds in the MIS 2 eolian sand at Bažantnica were triggered by repeated seismic shocks from the Vienna Basin Transfer Fault, acting on frost-cohesive sand.

decisive_move.sentence: Using the systematic fracture orientation (unrelated to bedding dip, inclined, uniform), the authors exclude slope mass movement and a periglacial wedge origin, which leaves the seismic trigger.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis is stated before data acquisition. The main wall was chosen for its abundance of structures and its orientation relative to the fractures, OSL sampling aimed to date the deformed horizons, and off-fault sandpits were checked with the fault location in view (p. 9, 17). The trigger claim faced orientation-based exclusions and a comparison with the VBTF stress field that could have failed (p. 26, 29). The mechanism rests on a plausible cohesion auxiliary, and the authors call for laboratory confirmation (p. 31). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Bayesian age-depth modelling with MCMC (Bacon package in R)
rheology and triaxial strength of frozen sands (Youssef and Hanna 1988; Arenson et al. 2007)
high-resolution gamma spectrometry (Canberra GC3020) for U, Th, K dose rates
abanico plots and kernel density estimates of equivalent doses

novelty_claims.quote: what is more, these are also absent from the recent reviews of soft-sediment deformation structures
no study describing how frozen eolian sand behaves when experiencing a seismic shock could be found in the course of the [...]
the present study reveals the underexplored potential of periglacial eolian deposits to preserve paleoseismological signals
An unexpected potential of periglacial eolian deposits to record seismic events is another noteworthy piece of information provided by the study.

limits: The supplied document is the non-peer-reviewed EarthArXiv preprint, not the typeset Sedimentary Geology version, and no review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence; differences from the published version are unknown. Sub-claims: the recurrence period of 142.6 ± 114.6 yr over 21 events is estimate_with_resolution, with uncertainty that the authors say exceeds most inter-event intervals; magnitudes below 5.5 rest on the absence of water-escape structures (estimate, weak); frozen-vadose-water cohesion is a 'likely option', not tested; the slide interpretation and the process model (Figs. 17-18) are best_explanation and marked tentative, and the authors call for laboratory modelling. The supplementary tables (age model, event ages) were not supplied. The paper does not report when the seismic hypothesis was first entertained relative to fieldwork (inference: prior reports of SSDS and the fault location likely shaped site and wall selection). The definition of an event (one horizon = one event) is a choice without stated alternatives. The off-fault sandpit check is reported without numbers or details. The magnitude inference and the comparison with the VBTF stress field depend on cited work (Decker et al. 2005), not on independent kinematic data in the Slovak segment.

disagreements.target: Fordinál et al. (2012a) and Kadlec et al. (2015): wedges interpreted as water escape structures
disagreements.support: The wedges show downward transport of material and formed in the unsaturated vadose zone, whereas water escape requires upward flow of a saturated sand-water mixture.
disagreements.quote: The wedge-shaped deformations under consideration were first interpreted as water escape structures by Fordinál et al. (2012a) and Kadlec et al. (2015).

disagreements.target: Literature on eolian seismites focused on liquefaction near the water table
disagreements.support: The authors document seismically triggered dilation and collapse structures in non-cohesive eolian sand without liquefaction, attributed to frost cohesion.
disagreements.quote: The majority of studies focus on the eolian sandy sediments deformed by liquefaction in the presence of water close to a paleosurface

disagreements.target: Steidtmann (1982), Loope et al. (1999), Ford et al. (2016): sliding of eolian loose sand yields massive structureless bodies
disagreements.support: The authors argue that freezing allows complex brittle and ductile slide structures in homogeneous sand, citing niveo-eolian analogues.
disagreements.quote: [...] of eolian loose sand usually results in large (on the meter scale) massive, structureless bodies
